note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LIGULE FIRST — OPEN THE INNER SHEATH
tiles.details: True inner translucent jagged membrane ~1–3(–4)mm reported in Williamson County D. ciliaris var. ciliaris key; still NOT directly photographed. Newly archived source-labelled exterior views indices 8–9 show sheath margins and blade junction with white OUTSIDE hairs, NOT the free adaxial membrane. Never use these white hairs to infer a hair-fringe ligule; this species has a real membranous ligule. Need opened inside photo with 1mm scale from corroborated specimen.
tiles.short: Whitish, translucent membranous ligule, jagged free margin, about 1–3(–4) mm in Central Texas.
tiles.status: HIGHEST PRIORITY — EXACT-SPECIES INNER LIGULE MACRO PHOTO MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · COLLAR, SHEATH AND BLADE HAIRS
tiles.details: NEW CC0 photo gallery index 8 shows green sheath wrapped around culm with long white exterior hairs, and index 9 shows actual blade/sheath collar zone. These clear partial PHOTO documentation of the outside junction and sheath hair placement. Neither confirms auricle absence from all sides or provides measured true free inner membrane. Observation is source determined D. ciliaris but graded needs ID, not an authenticated herbarium voucher.
tiles.short: No auricles; check which hairs belong to sheath/collar, versus blade surfaces.
tiles.status: HIGH PRIORITY — VERIFIED OUTER COLLAR/SHEATH PHOTO WITH REUSE RIGHTS PENDING

tiles.heading: 03 · FLOWERING HEAD — FINGERLIKE ONE-SIDED RACEMES
tiles.details: Existing local species panels 2–3 (indices 1–2) visibly demonstrate several clustered one-sided racemes. Distinguish the WHOLE raceme (flowering branch) from its individual overlapping SPIKELETS; existing macros panel 5 (index 4) confirm attached one-sided spikelets. Unlike diffuse fall witchgrass, all flowering branches here look like fingers bearing tight aligned grains. These gross panels are already adequate; don't waste this pass adding more duplicate distant heads.
tiles.short: Typically 3–7 near-fingerlike, one-sided branches densely carrying spikelets.
tiles.status: COVERED — REAL ATTACHED RACEMES, PANICLE AND SPIKELETS

tiles.heading: 04 · HIDDEN SIDE OF SPIKELET — UPPER GLUME
tiles.details: New CC0 source-labelled detached spikelet reverse-face index 10 has obvious pale and green overlapping surfaces, but the individual upper/lower GLUMES and sterile/fertile LEMMAS remain UNSEPARATED and unmeasured. Compare against original detached scale-view index3 and attached one-sided rachis index4. Carefully isolate upper glume from one ripe source-verified spikelet and photograph its full length beside a genuine 1-mm ruler; this is essential to discriminate D. sanguinalis.
tiles.short: Examine the reverse face: upper glume proportion helps separate southern from large crabgrass.
tiles.status: NEXT ANATOMY TARGET — TRUE HIDDEN UPPER GLUME AND DISSECTION STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · SHEATH/LIGULE COMPARISONS WITH CLOSE LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: D. sanguinalis is a VERY close look-alike. A genuine photographed, photographer-labelled, 1-mm-scaled D. sanguinalis subsp. sanguinalis spikelet dissection is ALREADY in gallery panel 14 (zero-based index 13): it is OTHER-SPECIES reference anatomy, NOT evidence of a dissected D. ciliaris glume. Panel 11 (index 10) is a real intact D. ciliaris reverse-face spikelet, but does not separately expose its upper glume, sterile lemma or fertile lemma. Compare both at the same scale once a vouchered D. ciliaris dissection is available; D. ischaemum remains unphotographed here. Gallery indices 5–7 are real D. cognata comparisons showing airy, widely branching panicles rather than ciliaris's one-sided fingerlike racemes. The exterior D. ciliaris sheath images 8–9 do NOT show the true inner ligule; a same-plant opened 1-mm-scaled membrane remains essential. Do not call the D. sanguinalis comparison a D. ciliaris anatomical confirmation.
tiles.short: Southern vs large vs smooth crabgrass; fall witchgrass has completely different flowering architecture.
tiles.status: COGNATA AND SANGUINALIS COMPARISON PANELS LINKED — MATCHED CILIARIS LIGULE/GLUMES MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · FINISH GATE — ABOVEGROUND FIRST; ROOTS LATER
tiles.details: ELEVEN physically archived D. ciliaris image records exist; TEN are represented in the current 14-panel teaching gallery (indices 0–4 and 8–12). The remaining archived overexposed base image is preserved but intentionally NOT used as anatomical proof. Three D. cognata comparison panels occupy indices 5–7, and one D. sanguinalis 1-mm-scaled labelled reproductive comparison occupies index 13. All 31 existing gross-structure markers are preserved; no new arrows. The uprooted roots in panel 11 (index 11) are genuine but do NOT demonstrate rooting from an aboveground node; panel 12 shows sprawling growth without confirmed nodal roots. The inner free 1–3(–4)mm membrane and separated D. ciliaris glumes/lemmas are still missing. No Hays-vouchered same-plant specimen or deployed Pages/mobile QA was verified.
tiles.short: Resolve true inner ligule, separate sheath hairs, then hidden glumes and lemma comparisons before root-node detail.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: SOUTHERN CRABGRASS (*Digitaria ciliaris*) — START WITH LIGULE: fold blade back to find a true whitish translucent MEMBRANE with JAGGED free edge, roughly 1–3(–4) mm (Williamson County var. ciliaris), not a tuft of external hairs. Next verify sheath/collar hair placement (sheath often hairy, blade comparatively sparse, no auricles); THEN follow 3–7 one-sided tight fingerlike flowering racemes and the paired mature spikelets on a winged axis. Hidden face of UPPER GLUME should be seen and measured to compare with nearly identical D. sanguinalis. Current eleven archived source-labelled photos cover habit, attached roots, head, exterior collar region and spikelets but NOT the inner true ligule or a taxon-correct glume dissection. Roots intentionally after aboveground anatomy. Introduced/non-native status and BONAP county review unchanged.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Start with panel 12: green leaves and long side-running culms on a rock, photographed in Maui. Visible sprawling habit, but NO independently verified roots at particular rock-contact nodes.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: True inner translucent jagged membrane ~1–3(–4)mm reported in Williamson County D. ciliaris var. ciliaris key; still NOT directly photographed. Newly archived source-labelled exterior views indices 8–9 show sheath margins and blade junction with white OUTSIDE hairs, NOT the free adaxial membrane. Never use these white hairs to infer a hair-fringe ligule; this species has a real membranous ligule. Need opened inside photo with 1mm scale from corroborated specimen.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Existing local species panels 2–3 (indices 1–2) visibly demonstrate several clustered one-sided racemes. Distinguish the WHOLE raceme (flowering branch) from its individual overlapping SPIKELETS; existing macros panel 5 (index 4) confirm attached one-sided spikelets. Unlike diffuse fall witchgrass, all flowering branches here look like fingers bearing tight aligned grains. These gross panels are already adequate; don't waste this pass adding more duplicate distant heads.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Against the installed D. cognata, look for tightly imbricate green or brown spikelets arranged on several near-parallel one-sided fingerlike RACEMES rather than fuzzy solitary units at the tips of a giant branching panicle. Against uninstalled D. sanguinalis and D. ischaemum, use the mature sterile lemma lateral nerves/prickles and measured spikelet differences, not whether the plant looks hairy. Goosegrass (Eleusine indica) can also make fingers but has flat zipper-like rows of many distinct florets and whitish compressed basal culms.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: ACTUAL CONNECTED ROOTS — Southern crabgrass lower culm and fibrous root system
panels.caption: Real uprooted source-labelled Southern crabgrass (*Digitaria ciliaris*) by Forest & Kim Starr. A dry basal culm continues into a densely fibrous crown, with robust roots and fine secondary rootlets. Notice the connected root system; do not identify the right-side structure as a confirmed rooted stolon node or rhizome. Hawaii specimen, NOT a Texas voucher. CC BY 3.0; uncropped EXIF-free JPEG.
panels.creator: Forest & Kim Starr

panels.label: LIVE SPRAWLING GROWTH — Southern crabgrass across bare rock
panels.caption: Real Southern crabgrass growing among rocks at Wailua, Maui, by Forest & Kim Starr. Thin narrow leaf blades and green stems run laterally across the stone, with rising sheathed leaves at multiple points. The source is a source-identified non-Texas photographed plant; don't claim any specific contact point in the photo has produced new roots without excavating it.

panels.caption: Shaun Pogacnik's Pennsylvania source-labelled late-season plant shows a low leafy tuft with narrow dry blades and several fine flowering stems. Image does not prove a woody or perennial underground base, or the diagnostic wavy leaf margin at scale.

panels.label: Fall witchgrass — isolated oval spikelets on threadlike stalks
panels.caption: Shaun Pogacnik's Pennsylvania macro shows elongated tiny pale oval spikelets individually situated on long, very slender purplish branch tips. This is useful opposite tightly packed crabgrass racemes. No exact spikelet length, hairy branch axil or lemma anatomy is measurable here.

intro: SOUTHERN CRABGRASS (*Digitaria ciliaris*) — START WITH LIGULE: fold blade back to find a true whitish translucent MEMBRANE with JAGGED free edge, roughly 1–3(–4) mm (Williamson County var. ciliaris), not a tuft of external hairs. Next verify sheath/collar hair placement (sheath often hairy, blade comparatively sparse, no auricles); THEN follow 3–7 one-sided tight fingerlike flowering racemes and the paired mature spikelets on a winged axis. Hidden face of UPPER GLUME should be seen and measured to compare with nearly identical D. sanguinalis. Current eleven archived source-labelled photos cover habit, attached roots, head, exterior collar region and spikelets but NOT the inner true ligule or a taxon-correct glume dissection. Roots intentionally after aboveground anatomy. Introduced/non-native status and BONAP county review unchanged.
memory_rule: CILIARIS = FINGERLIKE ONE-SIDED RACEMES AND CROWDED SPIKELETS. COGNATA = AIRY BRANCHES AND DISTANT TERMINAL SPIKELETS.
safety_note: Eleven physically archived D. ciliaris image records; ten species panels plus four explicitly labelled other-species comparison panels = 14 teaching panels, with 31 existing gross-structure arrow markers total (zero new). Roots and a sprawling habit are photographed, but not an actual rooting aboveground node. True free inner membranous ligule and a separated D. ciliaris glume/lemma dissection remain unphotographed. The 1-mm labelled D. sanguinalis panel 13 is OTHER-SPECIES comparison evidence, not ciliaris anatomy. Source-photo licensing and live Pages/mobile QA remain subject to their separate checks.
field_rule: Look for low sprawling aboveground culms and clustered digitate one-sided racemes, then expose the INNER whitish frayed membranous ligule. Distinguish D. sanguinalis with truly paired dissected glume/lemma specimens: the labeled OTHER SPECIES plate by itself cannot verify ciliaris.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Against the installed D. cognata, look for tightly imbricate green or brown spikelets arranged on several near-parallel one-sided fingerlike RACEMES rather than fuzzy solitary units at the tips of a giant branching panicle. Against uninstalled D. sanguinalis and D. ischaemum, use the mature sterile lemma lateral nerves/prickles and measured spikelet differences, not whether the plant looks hairy. Goosegrass (Eleusine indica) can also make fingers but has flat zipper-like rows of many distinct florets and whitish compressed basal culms.
